title: Should you always revise in the same place?

source.citation: Smith, S. M., Glenberg, A., & Bjork, R. A. (1978). Environmental context and human memory. Memory & Cognition, 6(4), 342-353. Meta-analysis: Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203-220.
source.finding: Students who studied a word list in two different rooms recalled more of it when tested in a new room than students who studied it twice in the same room.
source.caveat: The 2001 meta-analysis found that place-dependent memory effects are real on average but modest, and individual studies often fail to find them. The original task was memorising word lists, not revising a subject. The script says the effect is small and unreliable.

scenes.narration: Always revising in the same spot might not be the best idea.
The usual advice is one desk, one routine.
In 1978, psychologists had students learn a word list twice. Some in one room. Others in two different rooms.
Tested somewhere new, the two-room group remembered more.
One idea: memories get tied to where you learned them. And your exam is somewhere else.
But be honest about this one. The effect is small, and it doesn't always show up.
Today, revise one topic at your desk. Later, go over it in a different room.
